sysd-found-205.q: Why can one DNS name lead a local client and a distant client to different addresses?
sysd-found-205.a: With split-horizon DNS, a server that has both a private LAN address and a public one resolves to either, depending on the client. Local clients then reach it directly with lower latency, while internal DNS information stays separate from access over an unsecure public network such as the Internet.

sysd-found-032.q: Why do TLS, SSH and PGP use public-key cryptography only to share a key, then switch to symmetric encryption?
sysd-found-032.a: Public-key algorithms are far more computationally intensive than symmetric ones. So a public-key exchange shares a symmetric key, which then encrypts the data at higher throughput without pre-sharing a key.

sysd-found-038.q: Which HTTP method lets the client choose the target URI, and what happens if the same request is sent twice?
sysd-found-038.a: PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state with the state in the request, and unlike POST the client chooses the target URI. Repeating the same PUT updates the same resource.

sysd-found-168.q: What can a client safely do if the connection closes after it sent a PUT but before it read the response?
sysd-found-168.a: It can reconnect and retry, because PUT is idempotent and the effect is the same. It should not automatically retry a non-idempotent request such as POST unless it knows the request is really idempotent or can detect the original was never applied.

sysd-found-035.q: Why does HTTP separate safe methods from unsafe ones?
sysd-found-035.a: It lets automated retrieval by spiders and cache prefetching work without fear of causing harm, and lets a user agent warn the user before an unsafe action.

sysd-found-174.q: How can two parties who have never met agree on a shared secret key over an insecure channel?
sysd-found-174.a: Both publicly agree on a prime modulus p and base g, each picks a secret number and sends g raised to it mod p, then raises the received value to its own secret to reach the same shared value. An eavesdropper sees only the public values and must solve the discrete logarithm problem, which is hard for large groups.

sysd-found-191.a: A 401 (Unauthorized) says the request lacks valid authentication credentials and must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge. A 403 (Forbidden) says the server understood the request but refuses it, even with credentials that are insufficient.

sysd-found-062.q: Why were 307 and 308 added alongside 302 and 301?
sysd-found-062.a: For historical reasons a client may turn a POST into a GET after a 301 or 302. A 308 (Permanent Redirect) and a 307 (Temporary Redirect) avoid this, and 307 forbids changing the method on automatic redirection.

sysd-found-190.q: How does a cache work out a response's freshness lifetime?
sysd-found-190.a: It takes it from the first matching rule: s-maxage for a shared cache, then max-age, then the Expires value minus the Date value. If none applies, no explicit expiration exists.

sysd-found-054.q: Why did HTTP/1 clients open several connections to one server, and what does HTTP/2 need instead?
sysd-found-054.a: HTTP/1.0 allowed one outstanding request per TCP connection and HTTP/1.1 pipelining only partly helped, so clients opened several connections. HTTP/2 needs one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8.

sysd-found-041.q: Why does QUIC fix the head-of-line blocking that HTTP/2 still has over TCP?
sysd-found-041.a: TCP cannot see HTTP/2's parallel streams, so one lost packet stalls every transaction. QUIC's native multiplexing makes a lost packet affect only the streams that lost data.

sysd-found-172.q: How does Expect: 100-continue save a client from wasting an upload?
sysd-found-172.a: A 100 (Continue) response says the initial part of a request was received and not rejected. A client waits for it before sending a large body, so a request rejected on its headers wastes no upload.

sysd-found-066.q: What does proactive content negotiation gain, and what does it cost?
sysd-found-066.a: The server picks from the client's stated preferences and can send its best guess with the first response, saving a round trip. The cost is that describing capabilities in every request is inefficient and a privacy risk, and it limits reuse of responses by shared caches.

sysd-found-187.q: What happens if an HTTP/2 receiver's flow-control window is smaller than the bandwidth * delay product?
sysd-found-187.a: Receive throughput is limited and performance degrades. Timely WINDOW_UPDATE frames help.

sysd-found-075.q: What does the Vary header tell a cache?
sysd-found-075.a: Its value lists the selecting header field names, such as accept-encoding and accept-language. A cache may reuse the response only for a later request with the same values in those fields, unless the origin validates it, so Vary expands the cache key.

sysd-found-084.q: What does cache timing leak, and how does double keying mitigate it?
sysd-found-084.a: Cache timing leaks which resources were previously requested, since a fast load shows a site was visited. Adding the referring site to the cache key, called double keying, mitigates it.

sysd-found-048.q: How does SameSite=Strict help against cross-site request forgery?
sysd-found-048.a: CSRF abuses the fact that browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie. SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates CSRF.

sysd-found-180.q: Why is the first visit to an HSTS site still unprotected, and what closes that gap?
sysd-found-180.a: HSTS relies on trust on first use, so the first visit, and the first request after max-age expires, are unprotected. Browsers ship a preload list of known HSTS sites so that even the first request uses HTTPS, though such a list cannot scale to cover every website.

sysd-found-055.q: Why does the TLS 1.3 handshake take only one round trip?
sysd-found-055.a: The client guesses the key exchange algorithm and sends public keys for its guesses in the ClientHello. That takes one round trip instead of the two earlier versions need.

sysd-found-056.q: What happens in TLS 1.3 if the client's key_share is unacceptable?
sysd-found-056.a: The server sends a HelloRetryRequest and the client restarts with a suitable one. If no common parameters can be negotiated, the server must abort the handshake.

sysd-found-186.q: Which names does a wildcard certificate for *.example.com cover?
sysd-found-186.a: It covers only one level of subdomain: *.example.com matches sub1.example.com, but not example.com or deeper names.

sysd-found-051.q: How does If-Match prevent the lost update problem?
sysd-found-051.a: If-Match makes a method conditional on the current entity tag matching, and a failure gets 412 (Precondition Failed). Used with POST, PUT and DELETE, it stops one client from overwriting another's work.

sysd-found-069.q: How can a cache revalidate a stale response without downloading it again?
sysd-found-069.a: It forwards a request with preconditions built from the stored response's validators: the Last-Modified timestamp in If-Modified-Since and the entity tags in If-None-Match. A 304 (Not Modified) answer means the stored response can be updated and reused, so no content is transferred.

sysd-found-083.q: How is no-cache different from no-store?
sysd-found-083.a: No-cache means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation. No-store means a cache must not store any part of the request or response.

sysd-reliab-106.q: Why can't a hash function avoid collisions, and how do hash tables cope?
sysd-reliab-106.a: Hash functions are many-to-one, with far more possible inputs than output values, so by the pigeonhole principle a collision is guaranteed once there are more objects than hash values. Hash tables handle collisions with a collision-resolution strategy, most commonly open addressing or separate chaining.

sysd-reliab-001.q: Can a Bloom filter give a false negative or a false positive, and why?
sysd-reliab-001.a: It can give false positives but never false negatives. A 0 among an element's positions means it is definitely not in the set, while all 1s mean it is in the set or other elements set those bits by chance.

sysd-reliab-116.q: Why can nearest-neighbor search in a k-d tree skip an entire branch?
sysd-reliab-116.a: At each node it checks whether a hypersphere around the query, with the current best distance as radius, crosses the splitting plane. If it does not, that whole branch is eliminated.

sysd-reliab-115.q: Why would a ride-hailing design map locations along a Hilbert curve?
sysd-reliab-115.a: Mapping along the Hilbert curve keeps points that are close in one dimension close after folding, a locality property used to index geospatial location data. One Uber design applies it to run range queries that find nearby drivers.

sysd-reliab-013.q: Why prefer version 7 UUIDs over random version 4 as database keys?
sysd-reliab-013.a: Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits, so its keys are creation-time-ordered and new records land at the end of the key sequence. Random version 4 keys scatter across the sequence and hurt performance.

sysd-reliab-118.q: How can a peer verify a file from an untrusted source using a hash tree?
sysd-reliab-118.a: It gets the root hash from a trusted source, while the tree itself can come from any untrusted peer. A tree that does not match the root hash is damaged or fake, and another source is tried.

sysd-reliab-010.q: Why does HyperLogLog split the hashed values into many subsets instead of using one maximum?
sysd-reliab-010.a: A single estimate from the maximum number of leading zeros has a large variance. So the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the estimates.

sysd-reliab-003.q: Why can two nearby points have very different geohashes?
sysd-reliab-003.a: Geohashes that share a long prefix are close, but the reverse is not guaranteed. Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian lie in different halves of the world, so their geohashes differ greatly.

sysd-blocks-112.q: Why is round-robin DNS a weak way to balance load?
sysd-blocks-112.a: DNS does not check for server and network outages, so it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down or unreachable.

sysd-blocks-120.q: What happens to a user's session under sticky sessions if the pinned backend goes down?
sysd-blocks-120.a: There is no automatic failover: the backend's per-session information becomes inaccessible, and sessions depending on it are lost.

sysd-blocks-127.q: Why does the master-worker scheme scale badly to many processors?
sysd-blocks-127.a: It needs a high amount of communication, and the master acts as a bottleneck. Replacing the master with a task list shared by the processors helps, but is still insufficient for very large computing centers.

sysd-blocks-116.q: Why can a layer 4 balancer not route on content when a layer 7 balancer can?
sysd-blocks-116.a: A layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer and routes on network information such as IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. A layer 7 balancer works at the application layer and reads requests in their entirety, so it can route on content.

sysd-blocks-123.q: Why do load balancers use N+1 redundancy for failover instead of backing up every component?
sysd-blocks-123.a: Failover needs at least one component in excess of the service's capacity (N+1 redundancy). That is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a backup that takes over on failure (dual modular redundancy).

sysd-blocks-129.q: Which proxy hides origin servers from clients, a forward or a reverse proxy?
sysd-blocks-129.a: A reverse proxy: it sits in front of the origin servers so no client communicates with them directly, and the client never learns of the original server. A forward proxy instead sits in front of the client, so no origin server communicates directly with that client.

sysd-blocks-191.q: Why do microservices call for an API gateway?
sysd-blocks-191.a: Microservices typically expose fine-grained APIs unlike what a client needs, so clients would have to talk to multiple services. A gateway gives all clients a single entry point.
